clue.text: Long time oddly spent in Cape Town

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters of the place name are used up and gone, leaving the even ones

explanation.surface: Someone passed a long, strange stretch of time living in Cape Town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly spent' removes C, P, T and W from Cape Town, leaving the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An age or era of vast, indefinite duration, especially in geology or myth.

clue.text: Dessert wine that's no great shakes?

parts.note: afters is British slang for the pudding course
hock is a white wine from the German Rhineland

explanation.surface: A pudding wine is dismissed as unimpressive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no great shakes' usually means mediocre; here it is read literally as a smaller tremor following an earthquake.
explanation.definitionFit: A lesser tremor that follows the main earthquake, so its shaking is literally not great.

clue.text: Had looked grim when snubbed by father

indicators.note: snubbed means cut out, so the abbreviation for father is dropped

parts.note: to frown is to look stern or grim
Fr is the abbreviation for Father, a priest's title

explanation.surface: Someone had been glowering after being ignored by their dad.
explanation.definitionFit: Had in the sense of possessed, as in having had a car.

clue.text: Actor with the start of collywobbles during a rehearsal

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: during says the letter sits inside the run of other letters

parts.note: a trial is a practice run, like a rehearsal

indicators.note: start of picks the first letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A performer gets an attack of nerves during a rehearsal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' is only a link. Collywobbles is British slang for a nervous stomach, apt for an actor before a show.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as a noun, a theatrical is a stage performer, especially a professional actor.

clue.text: Barnet's decline shown in this clip

parts.note: Barnet (from Barnet Fair) is Cockney rhyming slang for the hair on your head
a slide is a drop or decline

explanation.surface: Someone's thinning hair is on show in this photo clip.
explanation.walkthrough: Barnet looks like the London borough, but it is rhyming slang: Barnet Fair, hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A clip is a small clasp that holds hair in place, a grip or barrette.

clue.text: Warning: group of distant relatives turning up!

indicators.note: turning up says the hidden letters are read backwards
group of says a cluster of letters is drawn from the following words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An alarm is raised as some far-flung relations arrive unexpectedly.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'Warning: group' as the definition, but 'group of' is the signal for letters drawn from 'distant relatives'; the definition is just 'Warning'. TRELA read upwards gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An alarm signal or warning, as in a flood alert issued to residents.

clue.text: Alarm loudly going off? That used to be correct

indicators.note: going off means the letter for loudly leaves the word

parts.note: to frighten is to alarm
f (forte) is the musical direction for loudly

explanation.surface: A loud alarm going off is questioned as being the right thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going off' looks like an alarm sounding, but it signals removal of F.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic verb meaning to set right or correct, hence the 'used to be'.

clue.text: Chapter introducing Tolkien's assorted characters as strongly-linked

indicators.note: assorted says the letters of the author's name are mixed up

explanation.surface: A chapter introduces Tolkien's varied cast as a tight-knit fellowship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'introducing' just puts C in front; the letters of TOLKIENS, including the S, are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Closely bound together, as a tight community whose members are strongly connected.

clue.text: What uses fuel up when covering miles?

definitions.text: What uses fuel up when covering miles?

indicators.note: covering means the reversed word wraps round the letter for miles
in a down entry, up means the word is written bottom to top

parts.note: oil is a fuel

explanation.surface: A riddle about a vehicle that burns through petrol over long distances.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: a large luxury car guzzles fuel on long drives, and the wordplay puts M inside LIO.
explanation.definitionFit: A long chauffeur-driven luxury car, notoriously thirsty for petrol.

clue.text: Improvement shown by class following course in religion

indicators.note: following puts the class after the religion course

parts.note: RE is religious education, a school subject
a form is a school class

explanation.surface: A school class after a religious education lesson shows progress.
explanation.walkthrough: RE stands for religious education, a school subject in Britain; FORM is a British term for a school class.
explanation.definitionFit: An improvement or amendment that changes something for the better.

clue.text: Fruit: taste before eating at home

parts.note: a tang is a sharp taste

indicators.note: eating says one piece swallows the other

parts.note: ere is a poetic word for before
in means at home

explanation.surface: A diner samples some fruit before eating a meal in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'before' looks like it orders the pieces, but it is a poetic word that does the eating.
explanation.definitionFit: A small citrus fruit like a mandarin, with deep orange skin.

clue.text: After end of spring-cleaning, part of house is tidy

indicators.note: end of picks the last letter of the hyphenated word

parts.note: a room is a part of a house

explanation.surface: After spring-cleaning, one part of the house is finally neat.
explanation.definitionFit: To make neat and smart, as when a person spruces up their appearance or a horse is brushed.

clue.text: Rags made from colourful tee-shirts

parts.note: red is a colour, so colourful here
tops are tee-shirts and other upper garments

explanation.surface: Old cloths have been made out of bright tee-shirts.
explanation.walkthrough: Rags are old cloths in the surface, but here are cheap newspapers; red tops are Britain's tabloids, named for their red mastheads.
explanation.definitionFit: Rag is a derogatory word for a low-quality newspaper, like the British tabloids.

clue.text: Ultimately humorist's trite cracks making you laugh

indicators.note: ultimately picks the final letter of the word that follows
cracks says the next word is broken up and rearranged

explanation.definitionFit: A nervous, suppressed giggle, a small laugh.

clue.text: Bomber to fly at speed round front of enemy lines

parts.note: to wing is to fly

indicators.note: front of picks the first letter

parts.note: a ton is 100 mph, so doing a ton means at speed

explanation.surface: A bomber flies fast around the enemy's front lines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at speed' is British biker slang: doing a ton is 100 mph. The Vickers Wellington was a British WWII bomber.
explanation.definitionFit: The Vickers aircraft was a twin-engined British bomber of the Second World War.

clue.text: Demanding substantial amount of money from former spouse?

definitions.meaning: needing a lot of care and attention, said of a fussy person

definitions.text: substantial amount of money from former spouse?
definitions.meaning: read literally, maintenance is alimony paid to an ex, and this is a large sum of it

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading takes maintenance in its British sense of payments to a former partner after divorce.
explanation.definitionFit: Describes someone needing lots of attention; literally, large alimony payments.

clue.text: Circulate and buy drinks for everyone

definitions.meaning: to move about or spread, as news does
in a pub, getting a round means buying a drink for each of the group

explanation.walkthrough: Buying a round, a drink for each person in your group, is a British pub custom.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrasal verb meaning to travel or spread widely; split up, it is a pub phrase for buying everyone drinks.

clue.text: Try lassoing wild rhino — most problematic

clue.text: A pathologist etc working here?

indicators.note: working says the letters are set in motion and rearranged

explanation.surface: A question asking whether a doctor and colleagues are employed in this place.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: medical staff work at a small rural hospital, and their description rearranged spells it.
explanation.definitionFit: A small local hospital in rural Britain, often staffed by GPs and visiting specialists.

clue.text: Route passing through a neverending valley somewhere in W Sussex

indicators.note: passing through puts the route inside the other letters
neverending means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: a dell is a small wooded valley
a run is a regular route

explanation.surface: A road winds through a deep valley somewhere in West Sussex.
explanation.walkthrough: RUN goes into A + DEL (DELL less its end). Arundel is a castle town in West Sussex, an English county.
explanation.definitionFit: A historic town in West Sussex, known for its castle and cathedral.

clue.text: Consoles groups called for jury service

definitions.meaning: control boards with dials and switches
a jury list summoned to court is called this

explanation.walkthrough: 'Consoles' looks like a verb meaning comforts, but it is a noun: instrument boards.
explanation.definitionFit: Control boards fitted with instruments; also the lists of people summoned as jurors.

clue.text: French writer has little time for America at first

explanation.walkthrough: 'has little time for' reads as dislike, but splits into three pieces; 'at first' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcel, the French novelist who wrote In Search of Lost Time.

clue.text: Subject to choose for hearing

explanation.definitionFit: A subject or theme under discussion.

clue.text: Figure there's time to tether horse

explanation.definitionFit: A polygon with nine sides is a geometric figure.

clue.text: Author has success in up-and-coming journal
